diseases.name: ARDS
phases: Early ARDS. At organ level, oxygen levels fall and both lungs show patchy infiltrates. At cellular level, inflammatory injury makes the alveolar capillary barrier leaky.

Established ARDS. At organ level, the lungs are stiff and heavy and the patient needs a ventilator. At cellular level, type 1 alveolar cells die, protein rich fluid floods the sacs and surfactant fails.

Severe ARDS. At organ level, much of the lung is flooded or collapsed, leaving a small working baby lung. At cellular level, hyaline membranes form and the lung circulation is squeezed by hypoxia and micro clots.
Critical ARDS. At organ level, oxygenation fails despite maximal support and the right ventricle is strained. At cellular level, fibroblasts begin to lay down collagen.
diseases.rxtext: Lung protective care. Low tidal volume and limited plateau pressure protect the alveoli, prone positioning improves matching, and avoiding fluid overload unloads the right ventricle.
links: High airway pressures raise right ventricular afterload
Prolonged injury leaves a scarred, high resistance lung circulation
Injured lung is easier to infect

name: RV
failure

rx.note: lower driving pressure unloads the right ventricle
improves oxygenation and lowers lung resistance
keeps the right coronary perfusion pressure up

complications.trig: Rising pulmonary vascular resistance from hypoxic vasoconstriction, hypercapnia, high plateau pressure and micro clots in the lung circulation.
complications.rev: Often reversible once oxygenation, pH and driving pressure improve. Prolonged ARDS can leave chronic pulmonary hypertension.
complications.org: RV failure, organ level. High resistance in the lung circulation overloads the thin walled right ventricle. It dilates and pushes the septum toward the left ventricle, so left filling and cardiac output fall.
complications.cell: RV failure, cell level. Right ventricular muscle cells are over stretched and their coronary supply falls under pressure. Stretch and ischaemia signals cut the force each cell can generate.
prog: Early. At organ level, pulmonary pressure begins to climb. At cellular level, right ventricular cells stretch a little and compensate by contracting harder.
Mild strain. At organ level, the right ventricle dilates slightly. At cellular level, stretch signals begin to weaken contraction.
Moderate failure. At organ level, the septum bows into the left ventricle and left filling falls. At cellular level, the muscle is squeezed and its coronary flow drops.
Severe failure. At organ level, central venous pressure rises and cardiac output falls. At cellular level, right ventricular cells are ischaemic and cannot generate force.

name: Baro-
trauma

rx.n: Low tidal volume, 6 ml per kg
rx.note: keeps each breath within the safe stretch range
lets leaked air escape and the lung re expand
adds distending pressure to healthy units

complications.trig: High tidal volume or pressure, heterogeneous lungs, ventilator dyssynchrony, high airway pressures during coughing.
complications.rev: Air leaks heal once pressure falls; a tension pneumothorax needs immediate decompression and is fatal if missed.
complications.org: Barotrauma, organ level. Excess ventilator pressure or volume tears the lung. Air escapes into the pleura and mediastinum, and a pneumothorax can collapse the lung and stop the circulation.
complications.cell: Barotrauma, cell level. Over stretched alveolar cells and their walls rupture. Mechanical stress signals also trigger inflammation, a process called biotrauma.
prog: Early. At organ level, airway pressures are acceptable. At cellular level, alveolar walls stretch but stay intact.
Rising pressure. At organ level, the plateau pressure climbs. At cellular level, the open alveoli are over stretched while stiff ones stay shut.
Overdistension. At organ level, small air leaks appear in the interstitium. At cellular level, alveolar walls tear and release inflammatory signals.
Air leak. At organ level, air collects in the pleural space and can collapse the lung. At cellular level, the torn wall allows air into the tissue and blood.

name: Fibrosis

rx.note: less ventilator injury means less repair scarring
drier lungs recover with less collagen
oxygen radicals injure and stimulate scarring

complications.trig: Persistent inflammation, prolonged ventilation, high oxygen, ventilator injury and failure of the early injury to resolve.
complications.rev: Early fibroproliferation can partly resolve. Established collagen scar usually persists, and many survivors have lasting lung function loss.
complications.org: Fibrosis, organ level. After the acute phase some lungs fail to heal. The lung becomes stiff and shrunken, gas transfer is poor, and the patient stays ventilator dependent.
complications.cell: Fibrosis, cell level. Fibroblasts proliferate and lay down collagen in the walls and air spaces. The thickened wall slows gas movement and the alveoli cannot stretch.
prog: Early. At organ level, the lung is still inflamed. At cellular level, type 2 alveolar cells begin to repair the surface.
Repair. At organ level, compliance is falling. At cellular level, fibroblasts begin to multiply in the alveolar wall.
Fibroproliferation. At organ level, the lung is stiff and gas transfer is poor. At cellular level, collagen is laid down in the walls and air spaces.
Scarring. At organ level, the lung is small and stiff and weaning is difficult. At cellular level, thick collagen replaces the thin air blood barrier.

name: Ventilator
pneumonia

rx.n: Head of bed up 30 to 45 degrees
rx.note: stops secretions tracking down the tube

rx.n: Subglottic suction and cuff pressure care
rx.note: keeps oral secretions out of the lung

rx.n: Daily sedation hold and weaning review

rx.note: the longer the tube stays, the higher the risk

complications.trig: Prolonged intubation, aspirated oral secretions, biofilm on the tube, immunosuppression and flat positioning.
complications.rev: Treatable with early appropriate antibiotics. Delay raises mortality and prolongs ventilation.
complications.org: Ventilator pneumonia, organ level. Bacteria enter the lower airway around the tube. A patch of lung consolidates, secretions turn purulent, and oxygenation worsens after a period of improvement.
complications.cell: Ventilator pneumonia, cell level. Bacteria colonise the alveoli and neutrophils and macrophages flood in. They release enzymes and cytokines that injure alveolar and capillary cells and fill the sacs with pus.
prog: Early. At organ level, secretions increase. At cellular level, bacteria colonise the tube and the airway.
Colonisation. At organ level, the secretions turn thick and yellow. At cellular level, bacteria reach the small airways.
Pneumonia. At organ level, fever returns and a new infiltrate appears. At cellular level, neutrophils flood the alveoli.
Severe. At organ level, oxygenation falls again and shock may follow. At cellular level, the sacs fill with pus and the barrier fails.

diseases.name: Acute pancreatitis
phases: Early pancreatitis. At organ level, the patient has severe upper abdominal pain and a raised lipase. At cellular level, digestive enzymes activate inside acinar cells instead of in the gut.

Established pancreatitis. At organ level, the pancreas is inflamed and fluid leaks into the abdomen. At cellular level, calcium overload and trypsin activation injure acinar cells and release cytokines.
Severe pancreatitis. At organ level, systemic inflammation causes shock and lung and kidney injury. At cellular level, cytokines make capillaries leaky throughout the body.

Critical necrotising pancreatitis. At organ level, pancreatic tissue dies and may become infected. At cellular level, small vessels clot, the cells die, and dead tissue releases more enzymes and signals.
diseases.rxtext: Early supportive care. Targeted fluids, analgesia, oxygen and early enteral feeding reduce organ failure.
links: Enzymes and cytokines from dead tissue drive shock
Lung injury and shock reinforce each other
Resuscitation and oedema raise abdominal pressure

name: Shock

rx.note: refills the vessels, guided by response
restores pressure once volume is replaced
raise the risk of kidney injury and death

complications.trig: Severe inflammatory response to gallstones, alcohol or high triglycerides, plus vomiting and third space loss.
complications.rev: Usually reversible with early volume and vasopressor support. Shock from infected necrosis is harder to reverse.
complications.org: Shock, organ level. Fluid leaks from the capillaries into the retroperitoneum and the third space. Blood volume and pressure fall, and organs lose perfusion.
complications.cell: Shock, cell level. Cytokines such as TNF and IL 6 loosen the junctions between endothelial cells. Plasma escapes, tissue cells swell, and low oxygen delivery pushes them toward anaerobic metabolism.
prog: Early. At organ level, the patient is thirsty and tachycardic. At cellular level, inflammatory signals begin to loosen the capillary wall.
Volume loss. At organ level, fluid collects around the pancreas and in the gut. At cellular level, endothelial junctions open and plasma escapes.
Shock. At organ level, blood pressure falls and urine output drops. At cellular level, tissue cells swell and switch to anaerobic metabolism.
Refractory shock. At organ level, vasopressors are needed and lactate climbs. At cellular level, cells are energy starved and begin to die.

name: ARDS
complications.trig: Circulating pancreatic enzymes and cytokines, large volume resuscitation, abdominal hypertension and aspiration.
complications.rev: Often reversible over days to weeks if the pancreatic inflammation settles.
complications.org: ARDS, organ level. Inflammatory mediators from the pancreas reach the lungs through the blood. Both lungs flood and stiffen, and the oxygen level falls.
complications.cell: ARDS, cell level. Cytokines and activated neutrophils injure the capillary and alveolar cells. Protein rich fluid enters the air spaces and surfactant is lost.
prog: Early. At organ level, breathing is slightly faster. At cellular level, neutrophils gather in the lung capillaries.
Mild. At organ level, oxygen needs rise. At cellular level, the capillary wall begins to leak protein rich fluid.
Moderate. At organ level, both lungs show infiltrates. At cellular level, alveolar cells die and the sacs fill with fluid.
Severe. At organ level, the patient needs a ventilator. At cellular level, hyaline membranes line the air spaces and surfactant is gone.

name: AKI
complications.trig: Hypovolaemia, shock, abdominal compartment syndrome, nephrotoxic drugs and contrast.
complications.rev: Usually reversible if perfusion is restored early. Prolonged injury can cause tubular necrosis or chronic kidney disease.
complications.org: AKI, organ level. Low volume and high abdominal pressure cut kidney perfusion. Urine output falls and creatinine rises, with potassium, acid and urea building up.
complications.cell: AKI, cell level. Tubule cells are short of oxygen and energy. They lose their brush border, detach into the lumen and block the flow.
prog: Early. At organ level, urine output is a little low. At cellular level, tubule cells are short of oxygen.
Injury. At organ level, creatinine rises. At cellular level, tubule cells lose their brush border.
Established. At organ level, solutes accumulate. At cellular level, cells detach and form casts that block tubules.
Severe. At organ level, the patient is oliguric or anuric. At cellular level, many tubule cells are dead and recovery depends on regeneration.

name: Necrosis

scene.lg: Yellow granules: digestive enzymes. Orange dots escaping: enzymes digesting tissue. Dark discs: membrane holes.
scene.s0: A pancreatic acinar cell. It stores digestive enzymes in granules and must keep them locked away.
scene.s1: The membrane breaks down and enzymes escape to digest the cells around it.
scene.s2: Calcium overload and failing mitochondria trigger enzyme activation and cell death.

rx.note: protects the gut barrier and cuts infection
removes the stone that drives injury
adds injury; delay and step up drainage is better
worsen tissue swelling and organ failure

complications.trig: Severe acinar injury with microvascular thrombosis, hypoperfusion and activated enzymes.
complications.rev: Dead tissue does not recover. The gland may heal around it, but necrosis can become infected and need drainage.
complications.org: Necrosis, organ level. Part of the gland and the fat around it die. Dead tissue releases enzymes and cytokines, can become infected, and drives organ failure.
complications.cell: Necrosis, cell level. Calcium overload and mitochondrial failure activate trypsin inside the acinar cell. The membrane ruptures and the enzymes digest neighbouring cells.
prog: Early. At organ level, the gland is swollen and tender. At cellular level, enzymes activate inside acinar cells.
Injury. At organ level, small areas are poorly perfused. At cellular level, calcium overload damages the mitochondria.
Necrosis begins. At organ level, areas of gland and fat do not enhance on scan. At cellular level, membranes rupture and enzymes escape.
Extensive necrosis. At organ level, a large part of the pancreas is dead and may become infected. At cellular level, enzymes digest the surrounding tissue.

name: Abdominal
compartment

rx.note: last resort when pressure stays high

complications.trig: Large volume resuscitation, ileus, retroperitoneal oedema and ascites.
complications.rev: Reversible with decompression. Delay causes kidney, gut and liver ischaemia.
complications.org: Abdominal compartment syndrome, organ level. Fluid and swollen bowel raise the pressure inside the abdomen above 20 mmHg. The diaphragm is pushed up, venous return falls and the kidneys and gut lose blood flow.
complications.cell: Abdominal compartment syndrome, cell level. High pressure squeezes the small vessels in the gut wall and kidney. Cells downstream lose blood flow, swell and switch to anaerobic metabolism, and the gut barrier fails.
prog: Early. At organ level, the abdomen is tense. At cellular level, small vessels in the gut wall are compressed.
Raised pressure. At organ level, the bladder pressure is above 12. At cellular level, gut cells swell.
Compartment syndrome. At organ level, urine output falls and ventilation pressures rise. At cellular level, tissue cells lose oxygen.
Severe. At organ level, kidneys, gut and liver fail. At cellular level, cells are dying and the gut barrier breaks.

name: Hypo-
calcemia

scene.lg: Violet dots: calcium outside the cell. Fewer dots mean less calcium. Dark discs: unstable membrane.
scene.s0: A nerve or muscle cell bathed in calcium.
scene.s1: Low outside calcium makes sodium channels open too easily, so the cell fires on its own.

rx.note: restores calcium and calms the membrane

rx.n: Treat the pancreatitis and correct for albumin

complications.trig: Calcium soaps in fat necrosis, low albumin, low magnesium and large resuscitation.
complications.rev: Reversible with calcium and magnesium. It usually settles as the pancreatitis resolves.
complications.org: Hypocalcaemia, organ level. Calcium soaps form in the dead fat around the pancreas and calcium falls in the blood. The patient has tingling, cramps and a long QT interval, and may have seizures.
complications.cell: Hypocalcaemia, cell level. Low outside calcium makes sodium channels open too easily. Nerve and muscle cells fire spontaneously, causing tetany and arrhythmia.
prog: Early. At organ level, calcium is slightly low. At cellular level, the membrane is a little more excitable.
Mild. At organ level, there is tingling around the mouth. At cellular level, sodium channels open more easily.
Moderate. At organ level, the patient has cramps and a long QT interval. At cellular level, nerves fire spontaneously.
Severe. At organ level, there is tetany, seizures or arrhythmia. At cellular level, the membrane fires uncontrollably.

diseases.name: AKI
phases: Early AKI. At organ level, urine output falls and creatinine begins to rise. At cellular level, tubule cells run short of oxygen and energy.
Established AKI. At organ level, creatinine climbs and urine output stays low. At cellular level, tubule cells lose their brush border and begin to detach.
Severe AKI. At organ level, potassium, acid and urea build up and the lungs fill with fluid. At cellular level, dead cells block the tubules and filtrate leaks back into the blood.
Critical AKI. At organ level, anuria and several complications call for dialysis. At cellular level, the tubules are largely dead and recovery depends on regeneration.
diseases.rxtext: Treat the cause. Restoring perfusion, stopping nephrotoxins and timely dialysis limit the complications.
links: Acidosis pushes potassium out of cells
Retained fluid and toxins both build up
Failing clearance leaves both acid and urea

name: Hyper-
kalemia

scene.lg: Yellow dots: potassium. Dark discs: leaky membrane. More yellow outside the cell means a less negative resting potential.
scene.s0: A heart muscle cell with potassium inside and a lower amount outside.
scene.s1: High outside potassium makes the resting membrane potential less negative and slows conduction.
scene.s2: Mitochondria make the ATP that runs the sodium potassium pump.

rx.note: stabilises the membrane but does not lower potassium
removes potassium in the gut slowly

complications.trig: Low urine output, acidosis, tissue breakdown, ACE inhibitors, potassium sparing drugs and potassium supplements.
complications.rev: Rapidly reversible with treatment, but untreated severe hyperkalaemia causes fatal arrhythmia.
complications.org: Hyperkalaemia, organ level. The kidney cannot excrete potassium. The heart is at risk first: tall T waves, a wide QRS, then ventricular arrhythmia or arrest.
complications.cell: Hyperkalaemia, cell level. High outside potassium makes the resting membrane potential less negative. Sodium channels inactivate, so cells fire poorly and conduction slows.
prog: Early. At organ level, the potassium is slightly high with no symptoms. At cellular level, the membrane potential begins to rise.
Mild. At organ level, the ECG shows peaked T waves. At cellular level, sodium channels begin to inactivate.
Moderate. At organ level, the P wave flattens and the QRS widens. At cellular level, conduction slows across the heart.
Severe. At organ level, the heart may reach a sine wave rhythm, ventricular fibrillation or asystole. At cellular level, many cells cannot fire at all.

name: Metabolic
acidosis

rx.note: restores the kidney's own acid handling
avoids the chloride load of saline

complications.trig: Failing excretion of acid and bicarbonate generation, lactate from shock, ketones and chloride loads.
complications.rev: Reverses as kidney function returns or with dialysis. Severe acidosis impairs the heart and the response to vasopressors.
complications.org: Acidosis, organ level. The kidney cannot excrete acid or make new bicarbonate. The pH falls, breathing becomes deep and fast, and the heart responds poorly to catecholamines.
complications.cell: Acidosis, cell level. Tubule cells normally secrete hydrogen ions and generate bicarbonate. Injured cells cannot, so acid accumulates and inhibits enzymes and the sodium potassium pump.
prog: Early. At organ level, bicarbonate is slightly low. At cellular level, tubule cells excrete less hydrogen.
Mild. At organ level, the pH falls and breathing deepens. At cellular level, bicarbonate generation falls.
Moderate. At organ level, breathing is fast and deep and the pH is low. At cellular level, acid inhibits enzymes and the pumps.
Severe. At organ level, the pH is dangerously low and the heart is depressed. At cellular level, energy production and calcium handling fail.

name: Pulmonary
edema

rx.n: Loop diuretic, if still making urine

complications.trig: Oliguria with continuing IV fluids, transfusion or salt load, and uraemia that raises capillary permeability.
complications.rev: Reversible once volume is removed by diuresis or ultrafiltration.
complications.org: Pulmonary edema, organ level. When the kidney cannot remove salt and water, volume overload raises pressure in the lung capillaries. Fluid enters the air spaces and the patient becomes breathless.
complications.cell: Pulmonary edema, cell level. High pressure forces fluid across the capillary wall. Type 2 alveolar cells that clear the fluid cannot keep up, so the sacs fill and gas exchange stops.
prog: Early. At organ level, there is mild weight gain and ankle swelling. At cellular level, the fluid begins to cross the capillary wall into the lung tissue.
Interstitial edema. At organ level, the patient is a little breathless. At cellular level, fluid collects around the alveoli.
Alveolar edema. At organ level, crackles are heard and oxygen falls. At cellular level, fluid fills the alveolar sacs.
Severe. At organ level, the patient is severely hypoxic with frothy sputum. At cellular level, the alveolar barrier has failed and the lungs are flooded.

name: Uremia

scene.lg: Green dots: retained uraemic toxins that bind the cell surface. Dark discs: membrane damage.
scene.s0: A platelet or nerve cell exposed to retained uraemic toxins in the blood.
scene.s1: Toxins disturb the membrane, so platelets lose stickiness and neurons signal poorly.

rx.n: Delaying dialysis despite encephalopathy or pericarditis

complications.trig: Prolonged oliguria with high catabolism and no dialysis; urea above about 150 to 200 mg per dL.
complications.rev: Reversible with dialysis, though the cause of AKI must also recover.
complications.org: Uraemia, organ level. Urea and other waste solutes accumulate. The patient becomes nauseated and drowsy, bleeds easily and may develop pericarditis or seizures.
complications.cell: Uraemia, cell level. Retained toxins disturb the membranes and enzymes of platelets, neurons and the pericardial lining. Platelets lose their stickiness and neurons signal poorly.
prog: Early. At organ level, the patient has fatigue and poor appetite. At cellular level, small toxins begin to build up.
Mild. At organ level, nausea and itching appear. At cellular level, toxins begin to affect cell membranes.
Moderate. At organ level, the patient is drowsy and bruises easily. At cellular level, platelets lose their stickiness and neurons signal poorly.
Severe. At organ level, pericarditis, seizures and coma can occur. At cellular level, toxins impair enzymes and energy in many tissues.

diseases.name: Acute liver failure
phases: Early liver failure. At organ level, jaundice, nausea and a rising INR appear. At cellular level, hepatocytes are dying from toxins, viruses or ischaemia.
Established liver failure. At organ level, the liver cannot make clotting factors or clear ammonia. At cellular level, hepatocyte mitochondria fail and the cells lose their glycogen stores.
Severe liver failure. At organ level, the patient is confused, bleeds and has low glucose. At cellular level, ammonia is converted to glutamine in astrocytes, which swell.
Critical liver failure. At organ level, brain swelling, shock and multi organ failure threaten life. At cellular level, the liver cannot regenerate fast enough, so transplant may be the only route.
diseases.rxtext: Specific treatment and ICU care. Treating the cause, controlling ammonia, supporting glucose and clotting, and early transplant referral.
links: Low glucose adds to brain injury
Bleeding into the brain adds to pressure
Failing hepatocytes lose both glucose and clotting factor production
Retained toxins and ammonia add to brain swelling

name: Cerebral
edema

rx.note: draws water out of the brain
water moves into the swollen brain

complications.trig: High ammonia, hyponatraemia, infection, fever, hyperacute onset.
complications.rev: Reversible if ammonia and pressure are controlled early; herniation is often fatal.
complications.org: Cerebral edema, organ level. Ammonia rises because the liver cannot clear it. The brain swells inside the rigid skull, the pressure rises and the patient may herniate.
complications.cell: Cerebral edema, cell level. Astrocytes convert ammonia to glutamine. Glutamine is osmotic, so astrocytes swell, and mitochondrial injury makes it worse.
prog: Early. At organ level, the patient is slightly drowsy. At cellular level, astrocytes begin to take up ammonia.
Encephalopathy. At organ level, the patient is confused with a flapping tremor. At cellular level, glutamine builds up in astrocytes.
Brain swelling. At organ level, the pressure rises and the pupils become sluggish. At cellular level, astrocytes swell with water.
Critical. At organ level, brain herniation threatens. At cellular level, swelling and mitochondrial failure damage the neurons.

name: Hypo-
glycemia

scene.lg: Pale granules: glycogen stores. They empty as the liver fails. Orange: mitochondria.
scene.s0: A hepatocyte. It stores glycogen and releases glucose between meals.
scene.s1: Glucose leaves the cell through transporters in the membrane, and needs energy to be made.
scene.s2: Failing mitochondria cut the energy gluconeogenesis needs.

rx.note: replaces glucose the liver cannot supply

rx.n: N acetylcysteine in paracetamol or non paracetamol ALF

complications.trig: Loss of hepatocyte glycogen and gluconeogenesis, reduced insulin clearance and poor intake.
complications.rev: Reversible with glucose; recurrent hypoglycaemia in ALF is a sign of poor liver reserve and a bad prognosis.
complications.org: Hypoglycaemia, organ level. The liver normally releases glucose between meals. In liver failure it cannot, so glucose falls and causes confusion, seizures and coma that can be mistaken for encephalopathy.
complications.cell: Hypoglycaemia, cell level. Hepatocytes lose their glycogen stores and cannot make new glucose from amino acids. Failing mitochondria cut the energy that gluconeogenesis needs.
prog: Early. At organ level, glucose is low normal. At cellular level, glycogen stores begin to fall.
Mild. At organ level, the patient is sweaty and anxious. At cellular level, gluconeogenesis slows.
Moderate. At organ level, the patient is confused and glucose is low. At cellular level, glycogen is nearly gone and mitochondria fail.
Severe. At organ level, seizures and coma may occur. At cellular level, the liver makes almost no glucose.

name: Coagulo-
pathy

rx.note: corrects deficiency that contributes to a long INR

rx.n: Plasma, only for bleeding or procedures

rx.note: hides the INR that tracks recovery and adds volume

complications.trig: Failed synthesis of clotting factors, platelet loss and consumption, sepsis and portal hypertension.
complications.rev: Recovers as the liver recovers. INR is a marker of liver function, so it is corrected only for bleeding or before procedures.
complications.org: Coagulopathy, organ level. The liver makes most clotting factors. In failure the INR rises and the patient bleeds from the gums, gut and lines, even though platelets also fall.
complications.cell: Coagulopathy, cell level. Hepatocytes stop making factors II, V, VII, IX and X and fibrinogen. Platelets fall and fibrinolysis is altered, so clots form poorly.
prog: Early. At organ level, the INR starts to rise. At cellular level, hepatocytes make fewer clotting factors.
Mild. At organ level, bruising appears. At cellular level, factor VII falls first because it has a short half life.
Moderate. At organ level, the patient oozes from lines and mucosa. At cellular level, many factors and platelets are low.
Severe. At organ level, major bleeding may occur. At cellular level, synthesis has almost stopped and clots form poorly.

name: Hepato-
renal AKI

rx.note: removes a trigger for renal vasoconstriction

complications.trig: Splanchnic vasodilation, low effective volume, infection, bleeding, nephrotoxins and the injury that caused the liver failure.
complications.rev: Often reversible if the liver recovers or with transplant. Renal replacement can bridge.
complications.org: Hepatorenal AKI, organ level. Vasodilation in the gut lowers the effective circulating volume. The kidney constricts to protect pressure, so filtration falls and the urine becomes almost sodium free, even though the kidney is structurally normal.
complications.cell: Hepatorenal AKI, cell level. Renin, angiotensin and noradrenaline constrict the supply to the glomerulus. Tubule cells are intact at first but run short of oxygen if low flow persists.
prog: Early. At organ level, urine output is falling. At cellular level, the renal arteries begin to constrict.
Functional AKI. At organ level, creatinine rises and urine sodium is very low. At cellular level, filtration falls.
Established. At organ level, urine output is low and solutes build up. At cellular level, tubule cells begin to run out of oxygen.
Severe. At organ level, the patient is anuric. At cellular level, prolonged low flow turns functional injury into tubule cell death.

name: Infection
vasoplegia
complications.trig: Impaired Kupffer cell function, low complement, central lines, ventilation and immunosuppression from the illness.
complications.rev: Treatable if recognised early. Infection is a leading cause of death and can worsen brain swelling.
complications.org: Infection and vasoplegia, organ level. Failing Kupffer cells and low complement leave the patient open to bacterial and fungal infection. Sepsis and vasodilation cause shock, and the infection can bring on brain swelling.
complications.cell: Infection and vasoplegia, cell level. Impaired liver clearance of bacteria and endotoxin lets cytokines surge. Nitric oxide relaxes vascular smooth muscle and the endothelium leaks.
prog: Early. At organ level, there is a low grade fever. At cellular level, Kupffer cells clear bacteria less well.
Infection. At organ level, the patient is febrile with a rising white cell count. At cellular level, endotoxin reaches the blood.
Sepsis. At organ level, blood pressure falls. At cellular level, nitric oxide relaxes the vessel wall.
Septic shock. At organ level, pressors are needed. At cellular level, the endothelium leaks and cells lose oxygen.

diseases.name: Acute heart failure
phases: Early acute heart failure. At organ level, the patient is breathless and the legs swell. At cellular level, heart muscle cells contract with less force and pressure rises behind the ventricle.
Established acute heart failure. At organ level, the lungs congest and the kidneys receive less flow. At cellular level, neurohormones hold salt and water and add load to the failing cells.
Severe acute heart failure. At organ level, fluid floods the alveoli and organ perfusion falls. At cellular level, myocytes are short of energy and calcium handling fails.
Critical acute heart failure. At organ level, cardiogenic shock appears with cold limbs and low blood pressure. At cellular level, myocyte death and microcirculatory failure drive a downward spiral.
diseases.rxtext: Decongest and perfuse. Vasodilators and diuretics relieve the lungs, and inotropes or mechanical support restore flow when output is low.
links: Rising pressure and falling output feed each other
Failing kidneys retain volume and flood the lungs
Short filling time raises left atrial pressure

name: Pulmonary
edema

rx.note: recruits flooded alveoli and lowers preload
dilate veins and lower filling pressure
respiratory depression leads to more intubation

rx.n: Beta blocker in acute pulmonary edema

complications.trig: Acute myocardial infarction, arrhythmia, hypertensive crisis, acute mitral regurgitation and fluid overload.
complications.rev: Often rapidly reversible with decongestion and afterload reduction.
complications.org: Pulmonary edema, organ level. The failing left ventricle cannot empty, so pressure backs up into the lungs. The patient is breathless and may cough pink frothy sputum.
complications.cell: Pulmonary edema, cell level. High pressure in the lung capillaries forces fluid across the thin wall and breaks it. The alveoli fill and gas exchange falls.
prog: Early. At organ level, the patient is breathless on exertion. At cellular level, pressure rises in the lung capillaries.
Interstitial edema. At organ level, the patient is breathless at rest. At cellular level, fluid collects around the alveoli.
Alveolar edema. At organ level, crackles are heard and oxygen falls. At cellular level, fluid pours into the air sacs.
Severe. At organ level, the patient is drowning in frothy fluid. At cellular level, the alveolar barrier has failed.

name: Cardiogenic
shock

rx.note: takes over part of the pumping

complications.trig: Large myocardial infarction, myocarditis, mechanical complications such as acute valve failure or septal rupture, and arrhythmia.
complications.rev: Reversible only if the cause, such as an occluded artery, is corrected quickly. Delay leads to multi organ failure.
complications.org: Cardiogenic shock, organ level. The ventricle cannot pump enough blood. Pressure falls, the skin turns cold, and the kidneys, liver and brain lose perfusion.
complications.cell: Cardiogenic shock, cell level. Myocytes lack energy and calcium handling fails, so contraction weakens. Inflammatory signals and nitric oxide dilate vessels and deepen the shock.
prog: Early. At organ level, blood pressure is borderline. At cellular level, ischaemic muscle contracts with less force.
Low output. At organ level, the pulse rate rises and the limbs are cool. At cellular level, calcium handling begins to fail.
Shock. At organ level, pressure and urine output fall. At cellular level, muscle cells run out of energy.
Refractory shock. At organ level, several organs fail. At cellular level, myocytes die and the microcirculation collapses.

name: AKI

rx.note: lowers filtration pressure and raises potassium

complications.trig: Low cardiac output, venous congestion, nephrotoxic drugs and contrast.
complications.rev: Usually reversible if the heart recovers; persistent low output causes tubular necrosis.
complications.org: Cardiorenal AKI, organ level. Low output cuts kidney blood flow, while venous congestion raises back pressure in the renal veins. Both lower filtration.
complications.cell: Cardiorenal AKI, cell level. Tubule cells are short of oxygen under low flow and congestion. Neurohormonal activation adds vasoconstriction and sodium retention.
prog: Early. At organ level, urine output is falling. At cellular level, tubule cells are short of oxygen.
Mild. At organ level, creatinine begins to rise. At cellular level, venous congestion lowers filtration pressure.
Moderate. At organ level, the patient retains salt and water. At cellular level, tubule cells begin to detach.
Severe. At organ level, the patient is oliguric with potassium and acid build up. At cellular level, tubule cells are dying.

name: Arrhythmia

rx.note: slows the rate with less depression than other drugs

rx.n: Calcium blocker or beta blocker bolus in decompensated failure

complications.trig: Ischaemia, electrolyte disturbance, atrial stretch, catecholamines and inotropes.
complications.rev: Often reversible with correction of the trigger. Unstable rhythms need immediate cardioversion.
complications.org: Arrhythmia, organ level. A fast or irregular rhythm shortens filling time and the loss of atrial kick drops output. A failing heart may decompensate within hours.
complications.cell: Arrhythmia, cell level. Stretched and ischaemic cardiomyocytes depolarise early and unevenly. Calcium handling becomes disordered, so electrical waves re enter and circle the muscle.
prog: Early. At organ level, ectopic beats appear. At cellular level, stretched cells fire early.
Atrial fibrillation. At organ level, the rhythm is fast and irregular. At cellular level, electrical waves circle the atria.
Fast rhythm. At organ level, the heart rate is high and output falls. At cellular level, filling time is short and calcium handling is disordered.
Unstable. At organ level, blood pressure falls and the patient may collapse. At cellular level, many cells fire out of sequence.

diseases.name: Traumatic brain injury
phases: Early TBI. At organ level, the patient has a depressed conscious level after impact. At cellular level, the primary injury has torn axons and opened cell membranes.
Established TBI. At organ level, swelling and bleeding begin. At cellular level, glutamate and calcium flood the neurons and mitochondria fail.
Severe TBI. At organ level, intracranial pressure rises and perfusion falls. At cellular level, cells swell, so more volume squeezes the brain.
Critical TBI. At organ level, the brain herniates and the pupils dilate. At cellular level, ischaemia and swelling kill neurons and brainstem function.
diseases.rxtext: Neuroprotective care. Head up, normal oxygen, carbon dioxide and sodium, adequate perfusion pressure, and osmotherapy or surgery for pressure.
links: Rising pressure pushes brain through the tentorium
Pressure surges trigger a catecholamine storm

name: Raised
ICP

rx.note: draws water out of the brain
water moves into the injured brain

complications.trig: Haematoma, contusion, diffuse swelling, hydrocephalus, hypoventilation, seizures and fever.
complications.rev: Reversible early with osmotherapy, drainage or surgery. Prolonged high pressure causes permanent ischaemic injury.
complications.org: Raised ICP, organ level. The skull is a rigid box. Bleeding or swelling adds volume, pressure rises, and blood flow into the brain falls.
complications.cell: Raised ICP, cell level. Injured neurons and astrocytes swell and endothelial cells leak, adding water to the brain. Cells that lose blood supply swell further.
prog: Early. At organ level, the intracranial pressure is normal. At cellular level, injured cells begin to swell.
Mild. At organ level, pressure is creeping up. At cellular level, the blood brain barrier starts to leak.
Moderate. At organ level, ventricles are squeezed and perfusion falls. At cellular level, cells swell and add volume.
Severe. At organ level, pressure is high and the midline shifts. At cellular level, ischaemia and swelling feed each other.

name: Hernia-
tion

rx.note: can cause coning when pressure is high

complications.trig: Large mass lesion, severe diffuse swelling, uncontrolled pressure and delayed treatment.
complications.rev: Time critical. Early reversal can recover the patient; established brainstem compression is usually fatal or severely disabling.
complications.org: Herniation, organ level. The brain is pushed across the midline and down through the tentorium. The pupil dilates, the patient becomes comatose, and breathing and blood pressure change.
complications.cell: Herniation, cell level. Displaced tissue compresses brainstem neurons and the vessels that supply them. Axons stretch and shear, and ischaemia stops their function.
prog: Early. At organ level, the patient has headache and drowsiness. At cellular level, pressure compresses nearby tissue.
Midline shift. At organ level, the brain shifts across the midline. At cellular level, axons stretch and the ventricles squeeze.
Uncal herniation. At organ level, the pupil dilates and the patient is drowsy. At cellular level, the oculomotor nerve is compressed.
Brainstem compression. At organ level, the patient is comatose with abnormal breathing. At cellular level, brainstem neurons are squeezed and ischaemic.

name: Ischemia
complications.trig: Raised ICP with low blood pressure, hypoxia, vasospasm, hyperventilation and microvascular thrombosis.
complications.rev: Reversible for a short time because of the penumbra, but sustained ischaemia produces infarction.
complications.org: Ischaemia, organ level. Pressure from swelling or low blood pressure reduces blood flow to injured brain. Regions around the injury starve and die.
complications.cell: Ischaemia, cell level. Neurons run out of oxygen and glucose, pumps fail, calcium floods in, and excitotoxic glutamate kills nearby cells.
prog: Early. At organ level, flow is a little low in injured areas. At cellular level, neurons switch to anaerobic metabolism.
Penumbra. At organ level, tissue around the injury is at risk. At cellular level, cells keep their pumps running but have no reserve.
Infarction begins. At organ level, areas of the brain stop working. At cellular level, pumps fail and calcium floods in.
Severe. At organ level, large areas are infarcted. At cellular level, excitotoxic glutamate spreads injury to neighbours.

name: Coagulo-
pathy

rx.note: reduces haematoma growth when given within hours

rx.n: Platelets and plasma guided by tests

complications.trig: Tissue factor release from injured brain, hypothermia, acidosis, dilution and prior anticoagulants.
complications.rev: Often reversible if recognised early. Progression of bleeding in a contusion can be fatal.
complications.org: Coagulopathy, organ level. Brain tissue is rich in tissue factor. Injury releases it into the blood and uses up platelets and clotting factors, so a contusion can enlarge and bleeding can progress.
complications.cell: Coagulopathy, cell level. Tissue factor from injured neurons and astrocytes activates the clotting cascade throughout the body. Fibrinolysis rises, platelets are consumed and clots that form are weak.
prog: Early. At organ level, tests are normal. At cellular level, tissue factor enters the blood.
Mild. At organ level, the INR starts to rise. At cellular level, platelets begin to be used up.
Moderate. At organ level, a contusion may grow on scan. At cellular level, clotting factors and fibrinogen fall.
Severe. At organ level, bleeding spreads and surgery is risky. At cellular level, fibrinolysis breaks down the clots as fast as they form.

name: Neurogenic
lung edema
complications.trig: A sudden surge in intracranial pressure that causes a catecholamine storm.
complications.rev: Usually resolves within days once the pressure is controlled.
complications.org: Neurogenic pulmonary edema, organ level. A sudden rise in intracranial pressure triggers a catecholamine surge. The lungs flood within minutes to hours, though the heart and lungs were previously normal.
complications.cell: Neurogenic pulmonary edema, cell level. Catecholamines constrict systemic veins and push blood into the lungs. Capillary pressure and permeability rise together, so the wall breaks and fluid floods the alveoli.
prog: Early. At organ level, there is mild breathlessness. At cellular level, catecholamines rise.
Mild. At organ level, oxygen falls slightly. At cellular level, lung capillary pressure rises.
Moderate. At organ level, crackles and frothy secretions appear. At cellular level, the capillary wall breaks and fluid enters the sacs.
Severe. At organ level, the patient is severely hypoxic. At cellular level, the barrier has failed.

diseases.name: Status epilepticus
phases: Early status epilepticus. At organ level, the patient has continuous seizures lasting over five minutes. At cellular level, inhibition fails and excitatory neurons fire repeatedly.
Established status epilepticus. At organ level, seizures continue despite first line treatment. At cellular level, GABA receptors move off the membrane, so benzodiazepines lose power.

Refractory status epilepticus. At organ level, muscles generate heat and acid, breathing is poor and the airway is at risk. At cellular level, calcium overload and energy failure begin to kill neurons.

Super refractory status epilepticus. At organ level, the patient needs anaesthesia and intensive care. At cellular level, ongoing excitotoxic injury kills neurons, and muscle breakdown threatens the kidneys.
diseases.rxlabel: Stop the seizure and protect the airway
diseases.rxtext: Stop the seizure and protect the airway. Early benzodiazepine, second line antiseizure drugs, oxygen and early airway control.
links: Seizure with a poorly protected airway risks aspiration
Hypoxia and heat deepen muscle injury

name: Hypoxia

rx.note: stops the seizure and the oxygen demand

rx.n: Intubation and anaesthesia in refractory status

complications.trig: Prolonged seizure, secretions and tongue obstruction, chest wall rigidity, respiratory depression from drugs.
complications.rev: Reversible if the airway and oxygen are restored promptly. Prolonged hypoxia adds to neuronal injury.
complications.org: Hypoxia, organ level. During a seizure the chest muscles contract and breathing is ineffective. The airway is blocked by secretions or the tongue, so oxygen falls while demand is high.
complications.cell: Hypoxia, cell level. Seizing neurons and muscles use huge amounts of oxygen. Red cells arrive less saturated, so mitochondria fail and the cells switch to anaerobic metabolism.
prog: Early. At organ level, oxygen is slightly low. At cellular level, seizing neurons use oxygen faster than usual.
Mild. At organ level, the patient looks dusky. At cellular level, red cells arrive less saturated.
Moderate. At organ level, oxygen falls and lactate rises. At cellular level, mitochondria struggle and cells switch to anaerobic metabolism.
Severe. At organ level, the patient is profoundly hypoxic. At cellular level, neurons are failing and are at risk of death.

name: Aspiration
complications.trig: Reduced consciousness, vomiting during seizure, unprotected airway, oral intake while drowsy.
complications.rev: Chemical pneumonitis can recover in days; infection and ARDS can follow.
complications.org: Aspiration, organ level. Gastric contents or saliva enter the airway during a seizure. Acid and bacteria injure the lung, causing pneumonitis or pneumonia with low oxygen.
complications.cell: Aspiration, cell level. Gastric acid burns the alveolar epithelium and capillary cells. Neutrophils flood in and release enzymes, and fluid enters the air spaces.
prog: Early. At organ level, there is coughing or wheeze. At cellular level, small amounts of acid touch the airway cells.
Pneumonitis. At organ level, oxygen falls a little. At cellular level, acid burns the alveolar lining.
Inflammation. At organ level, infiltrates appear and oxygen falls. At cellular level, neutrophils flood in and fluid enters the sacs.
Severe. At organ level, the patient develops ARDS. At cellular level, the barrier fails and the lung is flooded.

name: Rhabdo-
myolysis

scene.lg: Orange: myoglobin escaping. Yellow: potassium. Dark discs: membrane rupture.
scene.s0: A skeletal muscle fibre. It holds myoglobin, potassium and enzymes inside.
scene.s1: Energy failure stops the pumps. Calcium floods in and the membrane ruptures.
scene.s2: Failing mitochondria cannot restore the pumps.

rx.note: flush myoglobin before it blocks the kidney

rx.n: Stop the seizure and muscle activity
Monitor and treat potassium and calcium

complications.trig: Prolonged convulsions, hyperthermia, hypoxia, propofol infusion, statins and trauma.
complications.rev: Muscle regenerates. The danger is acute kidney injury and hyperkalaemia, which are preventable with early fluids.
complications.org: Rhabdomyolysis, organ level. Continuous muscle contraction and heat break down muscle. Myoglobin, potassium and creatine kinase flood the blood and the urine turns dark.
complications.cell: Rhabdomyolysis, cell level. Energy failure stops the pumps in the muscle membrane. Calcium floods in, enzymes digest the fibre, and the membrane ruptures and spills its contents.
prog: Early. At organ level, the muscles are tense and tender. At cellular level, the fibres use energy faster than they make it.
Mild. At organ level, the CK is raised. At cellular level, the membrane pumps begin to fail.
Moderate. At organ level, the urine is dark and potassium rises. At cellular level, calcium floods in and enzymes digest the fibre.
Severe. At organ level, the kidneys and heart are at risk. At cellular level, the membrane has ruptured and spills its contents.

name: Neuronal
injury

rx.n: Stop the seizure with antiseizure drugs
Treat low glucose and abnormal sodium

complications.trig: Prolonged seizure activity, hypoxia, hypoglycaemia and hyperthermia.
complications.rev: Early seizure control limits injury. Neurons lost after prolonged status are not replaced.
complications.org: Neuronal injury, organ level. Continuous seizures exhaust the brain. Swelling can appear in the hippocampus and cortex, and survivors may have lasting memory and cognitive loss.
complications.cell: Neuronal injury, cell level. Repeated firing floods neurons with glutamate and calcium. Mitochondria fail, enzymes digest the cell, and neurons die by excitotoxicity.
prog: Early. At organ level, the brain is still working. At cellular level, neurons are firing heavily.
Stress. At organ level, the patient is exhausted. At cellular level, glutamate rises around the neurons.
Injury. At organ level, swelling appears on scan. At cellular level, calcium floods in and mitochondria fail.
Neuronal death. At organ level, there is lasting loss of function. At cellular level, excitotoxic neurons die.

diseases.name: DIC
phases: Early DIC. At organ level, tests show a falling platelet count and a rising D dimer. At cellular level, tissue factor from the trigger starts clotting throughout the body.
Established DIC. At organ level, tiny clots form in many organs while clotting factors are used up. At cellular level, thrombin generation outpaces the natural anticoagulants.
Severe DIC. At organ level, the patient oozes from lines and wounds while organs lack blood flow. At cellular level, fibrinolysis breaks down clots, and platelets and factors are consumed.
Critical DIC. At organ level, major bleeding and organ ischaemia occur together. At cellular level, the endothelium is destroyed and microthrombi block the capillaries.
diseases.rxtext: Treat the trigger. Removing the cause is the main therapy, with careful blood products for bleeding and anticoagulation when thrombosis dominates.
links: Clotting uses up platelets and factors

name: Bleeding

rx.n: Tranexamic acid in DIC with thrombosis

complications.trig: Sepsis, trauma, obstetric catastrophes, malignancy and burns.
complications.rev: Reversible once the trigger is controlled. An ongoing trigger sustains the consumption.
complications.org: Bleeding, organ level. Platelets and clotting factors are consumed, so the patient oozes from lines, wounds, gums and the gut, and may bleed into the brain.
complications.cell: Bleeding, cell level. Thrombin generation uses up platelets, fibrinogen and factors. Plasmin breaks down the clots that do form, and the vessel wall has nothing to seal it.
prog: Early. At organ level, tests change but there is no bleeding. At cellular level, platelets are being used up.
Mild. At organ level, there is oozing at drip sites. At cellular level, clotting factors begin to fall.
Moderate. At organ level, the patient bleeds from several sites. At cellular level, fibrinogen is almost gone.
Severe. At organ level, there is major haemorrhage. At cellular level, plasmin digests the clots and the factors are exhausted.

name: Thrombosis

rx.n: Antithrombin or thrombomodulin in selected cases

rx.note: blocks clot breakdown and worsens thrombosis

complications.trig: Tissue factor release, endothelial injury, loss of natural anticoagulants and suppressed fibrinolysis.
complications.rev: Micro clots break down once the trigger is controlled. Large vessel thrombosis and purpura fulminans leave lasting damage.
complications.org: Thrombosis, organ level. Tiny clots form throughout the small vessels. Skin, kidneys, lungs and brain are damaged, and purpura or gangrene can appear.
complications.cell: Thrombosis, cell level. Tissue factor and injured endothelium start the clotting cascade. Thrombin makes fibrin, platelets stick, and natural anticoagulants such as antithrombin are used up.
prog: Early. At organ level, there are no symptoms. At cellular level, tissue factor begins to generate thrombin.
Mild. At organ level, the D dimer rises. At cellular level, fibrin forms in small vessels.
Moderate. At organ level, organs show early failure. At cellular level, microthrombi block capillaries.
Severe. At organ level, skin and organs are infarcted. At cellular level, natural anticoagulants are exhausted.

name: Organ
ischemia

rx.note: improves flow past partly blocked vessels
constricts vessels in a low flow bed

complications.trig: Micro thrombosis, hypotension, hypovolaemia, hypoxia and vasoconstriction.
complications.rev: Reversible while the tissue is only ischaemic; infarcted tissue does not recover.
complications.org: Organ ischaemia, organ level. Clotted small vessels and low pressure starve the kidneys, lungs, liver, brain and skin. Organs begin to fail one after another.
complications.cell: Organ ischaemia, cell level. Cells downstream of a blocked capillary lose oxygen. Pumps fail, cells swell, switch to anaerobic metabolism and die.
prog: Early. At organ level, perfusion is a little low. At cellular level, cells downstream have less oxygen.
Mild. At organ level, urine output falls. At cellular level, cells shift to anaerobic metabolism.
Moderate. At organ level, lactate rises and organs fail. At cellular level, cells swell as pumps fail.
Severe. At organ level, several organs are infarcted. At cellular level, cells are dying in large numbers.

name: AKI

rx.n: Contrast in a low flow state

complications.trig: Micro thrombosis in glomerular capillaries, hypotension, haemolysis and nephrotoxic drugs.
complications.rev: Often reversible if the trigger is controlled. Cortical necrosis from severe thrombosis is permanent.
complications.org: AKI, organ level. Micro clots block the glomerular capillaries and low pressure cuts renal perfusion. Urine output falls, blood may appear in the urine, and creatinine rises.
complications.cell: AKI, cell level. Fibrin plugs the glomerular loops and small arteries. Tubule cells downstream lose oxygen and die, and red cells fragment as they squeeze past the clots.
prog: Early. At organ level, creatinine is normal. At cellular level, small fibrin clots form in the glomeruli.
Mild. At organ level, urine output falls. At cellular level, glomerular loops begin to clog.
Moderate. At organ level, creatinine rises. At cellular level, tubule cells lose their oxygen supply.
Severe. At organ level, the patient is oliguric or anuric. At cellular level, many tubule cells are dead.

name: Purpura
fulminans

rx.n: Treat the trigger, such as meningococcus

complications.trig: Meningococcaemia and other severe sepsis, protein C deficiency and DIC.
complications.rev: Early treatment can save skin. Established necrosis needs debridement or amputation.
complications.org: Purpura fulminans, organ level. Purple, painful patches spread across the skin and limbs. Small vessels in the skin are clotted, so the tissue dies and may become gangrenous.
complications.cell: Purpura fulminans, cell level. Protein C and antithrombin are exhausted, so thrombin and fibrin run unchecked. Skin capillaries are plugged, the endothelium dies, and the skin cells downstream starve.
prog: Early. At organ level, small purple spots appear. At cellular level, protein C starts to fall.
Spreading. At organ level, patches enlarge. At cellular level, skin capillaries begin to clot.
Necrosis. At organ level, the skin blackens in the centre. At cellular level, the endothelium is injured and the cells starve.
Gangrene. At organ level, limbs may need amputation. At cellular level, the tissue is dead.
